purpose: Fluticasone helps reduce swelling, irritation, and inflammation in your body. It is used to treat nasal congestion and sneezing from allergies, asthma symptoms like wheezing and shortness of breath, and certain skin conditions like eczema or rashes. It helps you breathe easier and feel more comfortable day to day.
how_it_works: Fluticasone is a steroid that works by calming down the immune system's overreaction in your nose, lungs, or skin. Think of it like turning down the volume on the inflammation that causes your symptoms. It does not work immediately like a rescue inhaler — it builds up over time with regular use to keep symptoms under control.
common_side_effects: Nasal spray: runny nose, nosebleeds, headache, or a mild burning feeling in the nose. Inhaler: sore throat, hoarse voice, or a mouth/throat infection called thrush (white patches in the mouth) — rinsing your mouth after use helps prevent this. Skin cream: mild burning, itching, or thinning of the skin with long-term use.
warnings: Do not stop using fluticasone suddenly if you have been using it for a long time without talking to your doctor first. It is not a rescue medicine — do not use it during a sudden asthma attack. Tell your doctor if you have any eye problems like glaucoma or cataracts, as long-term steroid use can worsen these. If you get a serious infection, let your doctor know, since steroids can make it harder for your body to fight infections.
typical_dosing: Nasal spray (Flonase): Usually 1-2 sprays in each nostril once a day. Inhaler (Flovent): Typically 1-2 puffs twice a day depending on your asthma severity — your doctor will set the right dose for you. Skin cream: Apply a thin layer to the affected area 1-2 times daily as directed. Always follow your doctor or pharmacist's specific instructions.
